results.summary: This design displays a large collection of pride flags on a VGA monitor, with controls to select the flag by index or step through them. It is used by connecting a Tiny VGA PMOD and using the input pins to change the displayed flag. The design requires an external VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor. Silicon testing confirmed that flag switching works, though the index-based selection via uio was not tested.

This is a 16-bit counter built from standard cell flip-flops and custom half adder cells, designed in Magic. It increments when the enable input is high and resets when rst_n is low. The design is tested by providing a clock and observing the count on the output pins. Silicon tests show it works correctly up to 198 MHz, with errors in the top bit at 200 MHz.

This project implements a test of a manually placed circulating register intended for TinyQV's register file. It provides two 32-bit registers that constantly cycle, with a 4-bit wide interface for writing and two read ports for reading. The design is tested by writing data over 8 cycles and reading it over 4 cycles. It is notable for being a manually placed test structure for a register file.

This design is a register field made of 8 chains of 64 flip-flops, intended for studying the effects of electromagnetic pulses on initialized flip-flops. It is used by loading a pattern, injecting an EM pulse with external equipment like a Chipshouter, and scanning out the pattern to observe changes. The design requires external hardware for EM pulse injection. It is notable as a test structure for glitching experiments rather than a functional module.

This project implements a fuzzy logic system that estimates risk based on rainfall and soil moisture inputs. It uses triangular membership functions and three fuzzy rules to compute a weighted average risk value. The design is tested by providing sensor data via switches and observing the risk value on LEDs. It requires external switches and LEDs for input and output.

This is a simulation of a pedestrian traffic light controller that toggles between green and red lights with a countdown. It is tested by observing the output pins, where the lights swap after the countdown resets. No external hardware is required, but LEDs can be connected for visualization. The design is a simple state machine with a countdown timer.

This is an experimental controller for an autonomous robot, enabling sensor communication and path tracking. It interfaces with a gyro via I2C and a proximity sensor via UART, and controls motors with PWM and direction signals. The design is tested by connecting the specified sensors and enabling the robot. It requires external gyro and proximity sensors, as well as motor drivers.

This design displays a bouncing 64x64 Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA screen, with options to tile or double the logo size. It can be controlled with a gamepad to start/pause and change direction. The design requires a Tiny VGA PMOD and optionally a Gamepad PMOD. Silicon tests confirm it works as expected, including tile, double, and gamepad modes.

This is a ROM-less CORDIC engine that computes sine and cosine of an input angle using 16-bit fixed-point arithmetic. It interfaces via SPI to receive four 16-bit inputs and returns three 16-bit outputs. The design is tested with an SPI master, such as an RP2040, and achieves high accuracy. It is notable for avoiding ROM by generating micro-rotation angles with Taylor series approximation.

This design models a Quadratic Integrate and Fire (QIF) neuron using stochastic computing in bipolar format. It uses an LFSR to generate random bitstreams and implements the neuron equation with XNOR, MUX, and up/down counter. The design is tested by setting a 9-bit input value and observing the neuron's current value on the outputs. It requires an oscilloscope to view the output.
